Good question — here's the concrete payoff, not the plan. The short version: **after implementing this, a chunk of deadreckon that today only changes by editing Rust and recompiling becomes changeable by editing `config.toml`** — while the one thing that makes deadreckon trustworthy stays untouchable.

## The tangible surface you'd gain

Today, to change how deadreckon governs a run, you fork the source. After this, you write ~12 lines of config:

```toml
# ~/.deadreckon/config.toml
[seams.policy]
command = ["my-opa-worker", "--bundle", "rules.tar.gz"]   # your allow/deny engine
timeout_ms = 5000

[seams.catalog]
command = ["my-catalog", "--from", "https://models.internal"]  # live model list

[seams.hooks]
command = ["redact-and-ship", "--to", "datadog"]          # side effects per tool call

[seams.event_sink]
command = ["slack-sink", "--channel", "#agent-runs"]      # live run feed
```

…and `deadreckon run` now routes through your workers. Drop a line → back to built-in. Pass `--no-seams` → all built-in for that run.

## What each one buys you, before → after

| Capability | Today | After |
|---|---|---|
| **Policy** | What commands an agent may run is the OS sandbox + hardcoded Rust. Change it = recompile. | Every tool call is checked by *your* worker (OPA, Cedar, a Python script, a company service) returning allow/deny. The sandbox stays a hard floor under it — your worker can only *tighten*, never loosen. Enforce "no network," "no writes outside `src/`," "block `rm -rf`" on an autonomous run, auditable, no fork. |
| **Model catalog** | Context windows + pricing are baked in; a new model needs a deadreckon release. | Your worker supplies the catalog at run start. New models / updated context windows / your negotiated prices show up immediately. |
| **Hooks** | Per-tool-call side effects are fixed (snapshots/provenance/traces). Want redaction or Datadog? Fork the loop. | Your worker receives every `ToolCallStarted`/`ToolCallResult` and does anything — redact secrets, ship metrics, alert. Observe-only and non-fatal: a broken hook never breaks the run. |
| **Event sink** | Run events go to `events.jsonl` + the attach TUI only. | Every event is *also* mirrored to your sink — live run status in Slack/Teams/a dashboard ("turn 14 done · $2.30 · promoted"). `events.jsonl` stays the source of truth, so attach is unaffected. |
| **Thin↔thick** | One fixed shape. | A quick internal experiment (no seams) and a locked-down customer workflow (all four + compaction) are the *same binary*, one config edit apart. |
| **Long API runs** | Against a raw API provider (BYOK, not a CLI agent), history grows unbounded and silently overflows the model's context window — long tasks degrade or error, with no signal. | History is deterministically compacted near the context-window limit (keeps the goal/acceptance spec + recent turns, elides the middle, logs it to `compaction.jsonl`). Long autonomous API runs actually finish — and resume still works because it's deterministic. |

## The subtle win

After all that pluggability, **"the agent can't fake the finish" is provably still airtight.** You could hand someone a deadreckon with a custom policy engine, custom catalog, and custom hooks, and still truthfully say *"the acceptance gate is the one layer nobody — not even a plugin — can forge,"* with green adversarial tests proving no seam can write the marker, read the gate nonce, or alter the signature. That combination — *deeply customizable yet with an unforgeable verdict* — is the thing neither a framework nor the iii model gives you.

## What you would *not* get (so the value is honest)

- **It's not iii.** No live worker bus/daemon, no hot-swapping a *running* worker, no per-worker versioning or registry. Seams are per-call subprocesses resolved at run start. (The bus is explicitly deferred to V1.)
- **No human-in-the-loop per-call approval** — deadreckon stays unattended-first.
- **The turn FSM, the sandbox backends, and the gate stay compiled-in.** Only the four named seams + compaction become external.
- **Compaction is mechanical elision, not smart summarization** (no LLM in the loop).
- **None of it exists until it's built.** This is a brief — 11 phases, 42 depth tests, real multi-day Rust work.

## Where it leaves you vs. the article

Remember the scorecard from the evaluation: the iii post "won" on **runtime replaceability**, **uniformity/one primitive**, and the **thin↔thick slider**; deadreckon "won" on the **unforgeable gate** and **supervising whole agents unattended**. Implementing this **closes most of the gap on the three axes deadreckon lost** — policy/catalog/hooks/event-sink become swappable via one uniform contract, config-driven — **without surrendering the axis it won**: the gate stays non-swappable, now provably. It's the "adopt the lesson everywhere *except* the trust root" synthesis, made real.
